Stage 3c · specimen 8 of 8 · Coaches Portal, phone, true size · Ask 8b

The coach's side: the club's year never shows, and one bill must not disappear

Almost nothing in 3c reaches Aisha Rahman, 11U AA's head coach. The club's year-end never touches a team's own book, its season or any portal screen; a bill still reaches her named in the club's own words; the year's name never appears in the portal. One thing does reach her, and the verification found it: a club bill made on a season that then rolls over leaves her Club tab while it is still owed. It happens today; a September year makes it the ordinary case, because the club bills next year's costs in the fall, on the season that is ending. Drawn as a question for you, not as decided: it changes a coach screen.

What the code does

  • The Club tab reads the bills on the team's working season, both halves: it says so in its own comment.
  • The closed-season page's money shelf shows the statement's categories, not bills, so the unpaid installment is not there either.
  • The Money Overview's "Club bills due" lane and the Ledger's club schedule read every season, so they still list it, and their door opens the Club tab at a bill it no longer lists.
  • The coach can still say "We've sent it" (the write checks the team, not the season), but only from a screen that no longer shows the bill.
  • The club sees it everywhere (Allocations, Coming due, the team's account), and its roll warned about it once, when it started the 2027 season.

What else in 3c reaches the coach: nothing

  • The club's year and its name never show in the portal. A bill is named by the club ("Club insurance 2026–27" is the club's own words) and binds to the team's season, as today.
  • Closing the club's year locks the club's own books only. A team's own book is the coaches': it follows the team's season, and a coach's write is never refused because of the club's year.
  • New allocation offers only a team's open season, so a coach is never billed on a closed season again (S3C-09).
  • The year-end papers leave each team's cash out (specimen 5): it is read at load, never stored, and never stated as at the club's year-end.
  • The season doors stay the club's (Stage 2), unchanged: the roll still warns about money owed to the club, and never blocks.
Stage 3c · formatting check · done before you see the drawings

Stage 3c, checked against the Coaches Portal

Every 3c "after" frame was checked against the portal's written rules before this page was published: the table and list standard and its register, the portal kit, the design log's rulings (every one since 3b was drawn is listed below), and the screens as built, read in their code (the Budget, Budget vs. Actual, the Overview, the payee window and page, New allocation and the coach's Club tab). Three things the check found are put to you rather than settled here.

The rulings, and where each landed

RulingWhat it saysStage 3c

Put to you, not settled here

  • A seventh difference (Ask 8c): Compare › Against last year on the club's Budget vs. Actual only.
  • A form table, shared (Ask 6): New allocation's teams are a table whose cells hold the form's fields (a tick, and a Share input under By amount). The standard's "no controls in a cell" is written for tables that display records; no rule names a table that is a form. Tagged shared: the tournament redesign draws entry forms too.
  • A coach screen change (Ask 8b): an unpaid bill on an earlier season stays on the Club tab. Drawn on specimen 8 for you to rule.

Drift found outside 3c (recorded, not fixed)

  • Start from last year's plan copies a one-month line's stored label unchanged ("September 2026") while moving its date a year on. The screens show the date, so it shows only where a period has no date; the build fixes the label with the year work.
  • Two year readings use UTC timestamps (the payee page's first year, Allocations' "This year"); both go through the one definition in the build (S3C-01).
  • The "more than a year ahead" refusal on an entry or a transfer reads the server's calendar, not the club's day. Not 3c's; recorded.
  • D8a (the club's Payees as a window over its Ledger, like the coach's) is still the owner's call, undrawn; option A here works with Payees as a page or as a window.
Stage 3c · not drawn · listed so the build carries it

What Stage 3c builds that has no screen

None of these needs a drawing; every one has to be done before the 3c walks can pass. Ratified 2026-10-07; the build runs as two sessions, CLUB_TIER_STAGE3C_SERVER_PROMPT.md, then CLUB_TIER_STAGE3C_SCREENS_PROMPT.md.

  1. The migrations, each with the data dictionary and both snapshots in the same change. The club's year: its first month, and a row per year with its name, first and last day, and its close (who, when, the closing balance) and reopenings (who, when, why). A year can't stay a four-digit number: a change of first month makes two years share one, so the plan's lines need a key that survives it . No archive stamp on a book (Ask 8a). No close date on a season: no specimen reads one.
  2. The year's span moved, and every by-hand reading routed through it. The three definitions (the span, the year a day falls in, the year an allocation counts in) take the first month; the nine screens that work the year out by hand, the setup checklist, the payee report's "active teams", the club's quarters and the two UTC readings all ask the one definition . The one-definition guard learns to refuse a new by-hand reading.
  3. The lock, on the server. A write dated into a closed year is refused before it is made, on every club-owned book (the club's, a tournament's, the house league's), by every route that writes a line: an entry, a transfer, a receipt, an approval, a plan line or its dates, and an allocation from a closed year's line. Undo, Reverse and Void on a closed year's line are refused with the words drawn; a pending line from a closed year clears on the day it clears . A team's own book is never refused for the club's year.
  4. Close and Reopen, each one step in the database: the close checks the year has ended, records the closing balance it locked, and is refused if the year is already closed; Reopen only on the latest closed year, with its reason. Both re-checked after the write, as 3a's moves are.
  5. New allocation's server: a closed season is refused ; the line's year and the year's lock checked; the pasted ledger-entry id leaves the form (old rows keep theirs). The teams' list returns open seasons only, with the reason a team has none.
  6. The arithmetic gate re-proved across a year that starts in September, including a short year and the closed-year figures (the opening equals last year's locked closing; a closed year's Statement can't move), and the fixture rebuilt with a September year (owner's go before the reset).
  7. The old look's retirement in every file 3c rebuilds: the New allocation page (Rep Teams stylesheet, inline overrides, its own money formatter, the hand-built step bar), the payee report page if Ask 7 is A, and the payee window's always-editing form. npm run check:old-look:report lists what is left; each drop locked with --init in the same change.
  8. Help (/docs): the club's year, closing and reopening, the year-end report, New allocation from a line and from Allocations, a payee's window, and the coach's Club tab if Ask 8b is yes.
  9. Notifications: none recommended. Closing a year is the club's own act; nothing in it is news to a coach.
  10. Walks §G on the ledger, written as checkable walks on this hub's QA tab, one purpose each. The New allocation walk makes one from a budget line and reads it back: §271's W2 passed by ruling because no create was ever seen in a browser.

Recorded here, decided elsewhere

  • Stage 7: archiving a finished tournament's book, the one kind of book that ends (Ask 8a), with tournament money reaching the books.
  • /marketing: every sentence tagged on the specimens: the year window's consequences, the close question, the refusals, Reopen, the year-end report, the payee window's shortened note, the coach's band and caption (Ask 8b).
  • /docs: the help pass above.
  • Not 3c's: fiscal periods and closing entries (D2: not in the first release), bank reconciliation (its own project, both portals), tournament fees (Stage 7), families' money (Stage 5).
Stage 3d · read first · the code on 2026-10-08, after Ask 11 was committed

Where the last two money pages stand, and every door into them

You asked on 2026-10-08 whether 3c was meant to move Payees and allocations "away from pages and into drawers like how we manage similar pages in other areas of the portal". It wasn't (3c moved only New allocation and the payee's report), so 3d was added. Two club money screens are still pages: the Payees list, reached from Ledger › Tools, and an allocation, reached from five places by the plan's count. The code has ten. This screen lists them, the old addresses that must keep working, and six things this pass found that the plan's list missed. A team's account stays a page (Ask 6). What an allocation shows, and what can change

PartShown todayCan it change after it is made?
Its nameThe page's titleA route exists (a Rep Teams address kept from 3a) and no screen calls it.
The club's noteNowhereWritten once by New allocation ("for the club's own reference"), read by nothing, changed by nothing.
The line it bills from, and its year"budget line Diamond permits — city fields" in the toolbar line; the year nowhere on the pageNo. The year follows the line (or the first due date) and locks with it.
Each team's share and scheduleThe teams table, then each team's billNo writer. The read's own note says the terms "may change" on an open year, and the database locks them on a closed one, so the lock guards an edit nobody can make.
PaymentsIn each team's billYes, and these are actions, not edits: Record received, Confirm received, Undo (with a reason), Remind. A closed year's received payment shows the locked sentence instead of Undo.
Send remindersOn the allocation's toolbarIt opens the club's whole wave (every team, every bill), the same as the Allocations tab's.
ExportOn the allocation's toolbarA row per installment, with the team and each payment's method, reference and who recorded it. 3a ruled the build must not drop it. The Allocations tab's own Export is a row per allocation.

Old addresses that must keep working

  • Payees (accounting/payees, and ?payee=), and the report page 3c retired (accounting/payees/{payee}), which forwards there today.
  • An allocation (accounting/allocations/{allocation}, with or without ?bill=), and the Rep Teams address 3a moved (rep-teams/allocations/{allocation}), which forwards there today. Notices already in people's bells carry these addresses.
  • New allocation's old addresses (allocations/new, with or without ?line=) are 3c's and are unchanged.

What a head coach sees differently: nothing. Every door above is on the club's side. The coach's Money › Club tab and its bill room are not touched by 3d.

An allocation opens where you are, and closing it puts you back there

Ten doors lead into an allocation (the status screen lists them). Each could open the window over whatever it was pressed on, or move the treasurer to Allocations with the window open. The 3c walk answered this once already, for New allocation: “why do we have to leave the modal to allocate…”, and the line's window now turns into the form and comes back to the line. One rule for every door, recommended:

On this screen:

From a page (Allocations, Coming due, the Overview, Budget vs. Actual, a team's account): the allocation's window opens over that page, and × puts you back on it, where you were.

From a window (a budget line, a Ledger line, “behind the figure”): that window turns into the allocation's, the way Allocate turns a line into New allocation, and × turns it back.

From outside (the bell, an email, a bookmark, an old link): the allocation's address, which is Allocations with its window open, at the team's bill when the notice was about one.

Ask 6 · A team's account stays a page

A team's account gathers one team's bills, requests and history across its seasons, under a season band each. It is a view of many records, which the portal makes a page (or a tab), not a record you read and edit, so it stays a page with its back arrow, as the plan recommended. Only its doors change: a billed or received row opens the team's bill over the account page, per the rule above, and a request row keeps opening Payment requests with that request's window (unchanged). The bill's own “Open {team}’s account” stays a page link: from inside a window it moves to the page, which is where an account lives.

Stage 3d · not drawn · listed so the build carries it

What Stage 3d builds that has no screen

None of these needs a drawing; every one has to be done before the 3d walks can pass. Ratified 2026-10-08, every ask as recommended (owner: “I agree with your recommendations”); the build runs as one session from CLUB_TIER_STAGE3D_BUILD_PROMPT.md.

  1. The window kit learns two things. A named back for a level inside a window (“← Payees”, “← Diamond fees 2026”): shown at a desk, the bare ← on a phone, and the phone's Back goes there first (the kit's dialog floor already has the hook the coach's room uses). And, if Ask 7a is yes, a form that stands over another form, on its own layer between the form layer and the question layer.
  2. One allocation window, opened by every host. It reads its allocation by id, holds both levels (the allocation, a team's bill) and their questions (Record, Confirm, Undo, Remind), and tells the screen under it when money moved, so that screen re-reads its own figures: Allocations and Coming due, the Budget line, the Ledger line, Budget vs. Actual, the Overview, a team's account.
  3. The allocation's read and one write. The read adds the club's note (S3D-03). One edit route, under Accounting, takes the name and the note, refuses a blank name and a closed year's bill in words (the year lock's own refusal), and checks the member's team groups; the Rep Teams route kept from 3a retires. The terms (shares, schedule, teams) stay unwritable (Ask 7b).
  4. Send reminders leaves the allocation (S3D-04); the Allocations tab and each team's bill keep theirs.
  5. One joined band for every club money summary. The allocation's figures and its bill's open on the portal's money band (one frame, a hairline between figures, two-up on a phone), not separate cards; the club money kit's separate-card parts retire, a team's account joining the band too (recommended, no drawing needed).
  6. The Payees window replaces the page: Ledger › Tools opens it; the payee window (§283 W10) becomes its second level with Previous · Next; Delete moves to the end of the body; Merge and New payee ask as today.
  7. Every old address forwards in one hop (the table on specimen 4): Payees and ?payee= to the Ledger with the window; the retired report page straight there; an allocation's page and the Rep Teams one to Allocations with the window, keeping ?bill=. Notices already in people's bells keep working through these forwards.
  8. Notices write the new address, and the bell's label reader, which today names a notice “Open the bill” or “Open the allocation” from the page's address, learns it (its unit test pins both).
  9. The gates. The two retired pages' old look leaves (check:old-look, locked in the same change); the export catalog, which names the allocation page as its Export's home, follows the window (check:export-catalog); the layout sweep's three screens that point at the retired pages are repointed to the windows (and gain the phone); the UAT notices seed writes the new address; the 3c screens guard's Payees path and the payee tests follow the window.
  10. Help (/docs): Payees (from Tools and from the picker), an allocation (what it reads, the name and the note, a closed year's), a team's bill inside it, and where each door now opens.
  11. Walks, a new ledger section, checkable on this hub's QA tab, one purpose each: Payees from Tools; Payees from inside Add entry with the typing kept; merging Mizuno Canada Ltd. into Mizuno Canada (a write, read back on the Ledger); an allocation from every door, each closing back where it started; renaming one and reading the coach's Club tab; a closed year's allocation; and the phone for each.

Recorded here, decided elsewhere

  • Changing a bill's terms after it is made (a team's share, the schedule, which teams): not 3d (Ask 7b). If a club needs it, it is its own item with its own drawing, because it moves received payments, a team's own schedule, the line's “left” and what each coach was told.
  • /marketing: the name's hint, the closed year's line for a bill, and the help words.
  • /docs: the help pass above.
  • Not 3d's: a team's account stays a page (Ask 6); New allocation and the payee window's words are 3c's and are not redrawn.
Stage 6 · read from the code on 2026-10-08, before anything was drawn

Where the venues stand: three books, two clash checks, one program with none

Stage 6 draws four things, in this order of value: one venue book, one clash check across every program, the club calendar, and the Venue library fixed and redrawn. Every sentence on this screen was re-read in the code today. Four places where the plan’s §4D was out of date are corrected below, and the counts are in the notes. One correction changes the shape of the stage. The prompt counted clashes between programs: rep × league, rep × tournament and league × tournament. But the club the first release is for is a rep club with no house league, and its most likely double-booking is two of its own teams on one diamond. That is rep × rep, so it is counted too, and the check covers it.

On this screen:

The three venue books, as the code holds them today

The club’s Venue library

  • Venues, each with its facilities (diamonds, fields, courts, rinks…), one list per club. League, Club and Club · Association plans.
  • House league points at it directly: a league game or practice holds the venue and the facility it was given.
  • Saving needs the tournament permission, so only the owner and an admin can save; a league admin cannot (D02).
  • Delete is final, with no in-use check, and every house-league game on that venue silently loses it (S6-08).

A tournament’s own copy

  • “Import from Library” copies a venue and its facilities into the tournament and stamps where it came from.
  • Nothing ever reads that stamp. A clone drops it, “import from a past tournament” drops it, and importing twice makes two copies.
  • The setup wizard’s venue search offers other tournaments’ copies, never the library (a Tournament Stage 5 finding, recorded there).

Each team’s place book (Coaches Portal)

  • Built 2026-09-21: up to 100 places per team, each with an address, a usual diamond and a note, reached by typing in Location.
  • An event keeps its own copy of name, address and diamond, plus a link to the place.
  • The diamond is free text (“Diamond 2”). Nothing links a place or an event to a club venue, and Arrival & Places ruled that on purpose (“the admin’s library stays admin’s”). Ask 1 reverses that for club teams.

Every clash check today

The one shared piece is the “same surface?” answer both engines use. It is module-agnostic, but a league id and a tournament id come from different tables, so they can never match. Typed words never match a picked diamond. The clock: tournaments store a local date and time, while league and rep events store instants. The cross-program check compares instants and turns a tournament game into one with the conversion the live-score code already uses.

Dev has no clash to count, because no club has a venue to clash on. The case therefore rests on three things. The club’s first season, when its teams share three or four diamonds. The demo’s weekly double-booking, which the seed writes and nothing has ever flagged. And the release target itself, a rep club whose clashes are between its own teams. ⚠ The test club (“UAT Rep Club”) has no venues, no places and no event on a venue: the walks need venues seeded as an additive step, never a reset.

Corrections to the plan’s §4D (re-read today)

  • D03: the per-program admin schedule it cites is gone. The admin’s read-only team schedule already files days in the platform’s zone. The device clock survives in three week/month groupings: the coach schedule, the house-league admin schedule, and the public league schedule. The public one groups by the server’s clock, which is UTC on the host, so a Sunday game after 8 p.m. can file into next week (S6-12).
  • D05: the old sidebar it cites no longer exists. The doors today are the rail (“Venue library”, Organization group), the house-league schedule’s “Set up your diamonds once”, and a “Venues” tile on the Organization page with no plan gate (S6-11).
  • D07: the calendar export’s “STUB” header was already trued on 2026-09-25. The team-wide feed is still dead: nothing ever makes its link. The help article still promises a subscribable link “in a future release”.
  • Time: there is no per-club time zone. Every org runs on one platform setting, Eastern (Toronto). “The club’s zone” means that setting today.
Stage 6 · specimen 1 · a head coach in a club · Coaches Portal, the Add Event window (640 px) and a phone (390 px) · Asks 1 and 2

A head coach picks one of the club’s diamonds, and hears about a clash before saving

Priya Nair coaches 13U AAA in UAT Rep Club. She adds a Tuesday practice at Lions Park, Diamond 2, 6:00 to 8:00 p.m. 14U AA already practises there from 5:30 to 7:30. Today nothing on the form can know that: her “Lions Park” is a row in her team’s own place book, its diamond is the words “Diamond 2”, and 14U AA’s is another team’s words. This reverses a ruling. Arrival & Places (2026-09-21, §5 “Not built, on purpose”) kept the club’s venue library away from coaches: “admin’s org_venues stays admin’s”. Its reason was a coach’s own convenience: a book the coach owns, with nothing to wait for from the club. That reason still holds for a team outside a club, and for every place a club doesn’t own. It does not answer a clash between two of the club’s own teams, which a team’s private book can never see. So Ask 1 is asked as its own question. venues drawn, not seeded

Stage 6 · specimen 2 · the rule every program’s line is drawn from · Asks 3 and 4

What counts as a clash, in one clock, and where a program’s own refusal stays

One rule, written before any line is drawn, so the build can put it in one place and test it once. The writers on the previous screen all call it. Then the harder question: house league and tournaments already refuse some of their own double-bookings. Stage 6 proposes that every new comparison only warns. So two rules will sit side by side on the same diamond, and this screen says so plainly rather than leaving it to be found.

On this screen:
RecommendedThe rule

Same venue, same facility, overlapping time

Ask 3
CaseWhat the line saysWhy
Same venue, same facility, the times overlap“Diamond 2 is booked by 14U AA practice, 5:30–7:30 p.m.”The only exact case. Overlap means one starts before the other ends: a 6:00 end and a 6:00 start do not clash.
Same venue, the facility not set on one sideSofter: “Lions Park is busy then: … Pick a diamond to be sure.”It may be another diamond. The line asks for the one fact that settles it.
A place that isn’t the club’s (a team’s own place, typed words)Never compared. In a club with a library: “Not one of the club’s venues, so it isn’t checked for clashes.”Words can’t be trusted to mean the same diamond (house league already treats typed words as a weak warning, and a picked diamond never matches words). Saying so in place is what keeps a coach from assuming a silent form means a free diamond.
CancelledNever clashes.As every engine does today.
PostponedA postponed league game never clashes at its old time; it clashes once it has a new one.As house league does today. A rep event has no postponed state: a postponement is a move, so it clashes at its new time.
A rep event with no endCounted as 90 minutes.House league and tournaments both assume 90 already. The coach’s form fills an end two hours after the start, so a missing end is a blanked field, an import, or an older event: 119 of 259 timed rep events on dev.
A tournament gameIts own length: the game’s, else its division’s, else the tournament’s, else 90 minutes.The tournament’s own chain, read once. Its buffer stays inside the tournament: across programs, only real overlap counts.
A team’s copy of its own tournament gameNever compared with that game.The tournament writes its games into each linked team’s schedule. Without this rule, every game a club team plays in the club’s own tournament would clash with itself.
A team against itselfNo line.Two of a team’s own bookings at once is a schedule mistake, not a diamond question (the coach sees both on the schedule).
An outside tournament (dates only)Never compared.It holds no venue and no time of day.

The word

The rule is the same for every sport: a venue and one of its facilities. What a line or a label says is the sport’s own word, read from the team’s, the league season’s or the tournament’s sport: “Diamond 2 is booked by …” and “Pick a diamond to be sure” for softball and baseball, “Court 2 …” and “Pick a court” for basketball, “Field” when a sport has none. Nothing on a Stage 6 screen writes the word in: it is the switch the schedule forms and house league’s “Set up your diamonds once” already read (owner, 2026-10-08). These drawings show a softball club, so they say diamond.

The clock

Every booking is compared as a moment in time. House-league and rep events are stored that way already. A tournament game’s date and time are read in the platform’s zone (Eastern, Toronto), daylight saving included, with the same conversion the live-score screens use. ⚠ There is no per-club zone: a club outside Eastern time would compare correctly with itself, but every time it is shown would be Eastern (Ask 7).

RecommendedRefuse or warn, by pair

Each program keeps its own refusal; everything that crosses a boundary warns

Ask 4
The two bookingsTodayProposed
Two house-league games or practicesRefused, on the server, after CreateStill refused. Only where it says so moves: under the Diamond field, before Create (specimen 3).

A club team and a club tournament gameNothingWarns, on both forms
A house-league booking and a club tournament gameNothingWarns, on both forms

Said plainly: on Kinsmen Park, Diamond B, Tuesday at 6:00 p.m., the league admin who books a second league game there is refused. If the diamond is held by 11U AA’s practice instead, the same game saves with an amber line. That is deliberate. A double-booked league diamond is the league’s own mistake, which the league can always fix. A diamond shared with another program is a question between two people with equal claims, and a form refusing one of them would hand one volunteer a veto over another’s schedule. The club calendar is where the club sees both and settles it.

Not recommended, drawn as the alternatives: (b) refuse every exact clash everywhere. It is the tidiest rule, but it makes a coach’s practice depend on whether the house league saved first, and on the day the club has permits the refusal would be wrong half the time. (c) Warn everywhere, retiring house league’s refusal: a change to a working rule this stage has no evidence for.

Stage 6 · specimen 6 · the club admin · Organization › Venue library, true size (960 today, 1200 proposed) · Ask 9

The Venue library saves for the people who schedule, and says what each venue holds

Once the coach’s picker reads it, the library is the club’s one venue book, and it has to hold up to that. Today saving needs the tournament permission, so only the owner and an admin can save. The league admin, whom house league sends here, is refused. A failed load reads as an empty library. Delete is final and checks nothing, and every house-league game on that venue silently loses it. A facility can’t be renamed, though the server allows it. And the copy names only tournaments. Every writer runs the check, each with a test

  • Rep teams: add one event; add a weekly series (every date); edit, move or un-cancel one event; edit a series (this and future, all); the schedule file import (a warning per row); the place book’s “Also update the upcoming events” (a summary of what landed on a club booking). The tournament mirror is skipped and tested as skipped: it must never compare a team’s copy of a game with the game.
  • House league: add and edit a game; add a practice (single and series); the season generator (counted in its existing after-save summary). Each keeps its own refusal against league bookings and adds the cross-program warning.
  • Tournaments: add and edit a game; drag on the timeline; the pool-play generator; playoffs; the rain-delay shift (a database function today, which needs its own call after it runs); field lanes resolved; the schedule import. Each returns the cross-program warnings. None changes the tournament’s own rule.
  • One rule, one place: the comparison lives beside the existing “same surface?” answer, and one list of cases (the rule screen’s table) is its unit test. A guard test fails if a new writer of an event’s time or place appears without calling it.
  • The permit hook: the check returns findings with a kind (“booked by”, “busy then”), so Stage 10 adds “outside the club’s permit” without changing a caller.

The data the build adds (with its dictionary lines and snapshot refresh; production order recorded)

  • An event’s club venue and diamond: two optional links on a rep event, the same two a house-league game holds. This replaces the plan’s “a place references a venue”, because the facility changes game by game.
  • Archive: the venue table’s existing “active” column, used at last, and a facility’s equivalent if a facility can archive.
  • The tournament copy’s link: kept by a clone and by import-from-past, plus the missing index on the facility copy’s link.
  • The database rule: members read venues, and only the server writes them.
  • Indexes for the clash lookup: rep events by club and start time.

The scorekeeper opens on the phone’s day, not the event’s; a volunteer east of the event sees tomorrow’s games after 7 p.m.The scorekeeperVolunteersTournament redesign
“LIVE” follows its own rule: an unscored game in progress isn’t live, and a submitted score stays LIVE all day.The coach’s tournament recordCoaches at a tournamentStage 7 (the record is drawn there)

C6-01 and C6-02 were confirmed by running the screens’ own date code in the coach’s time zone and two others; none was changed. The coach’s week arrow and the free portal’s clock reach only coaches outside Eastern time today; the month-end skip and the Overview’s day-early card reach everyone.

Found on the way

What the plan’s list missed

Ask 20.
FoundWhy it mattersWhere it is asked
A41’s “one shape” was never built, and the rule that would pick it doesn’t apply. The club calendar was committed first (Oct 9, 6:18 p.m.); the tournament’s Day three and a half hours later. The Day didn’t wear the club’s card; it wore the admin kit’s row, which is older than both. The club calendar draws a booking three ways of its own.“Whichever builds first” would make the club’s table the shared part. The row both should wear already exists, and the Day already wears it.Ask 5
One choice of view, three looks: the portal’s olive switch and the admin kit’s black switch on the same shared toolbar, and the tournament’s olive View pill.An admin who also coaches crosses it daily.Ask 13
Three answers to “which clock?” “Times in Eastern time.” (written into the club calendar), “All times are local.” (the public tournament), and silence everywhere else.“Local” to a family reading at home means their own clock; the times are the event’s.Ask 10
The club calendar hides cancelled and postponed bookings.A called-off game and a never-booked slot look the same.Ask 9
Stage 11’s draft grid can’t be the club calendar’s Week. The Week stacks bookings as cards by day; a scheduler hands out time, and needs the hours and the empty slots on the page.The plan says the grid “is the club calendar’s Week view”. Drawn that way, it couldn’t show a free slot.Ask 18
Today is drawn five ways (an olive edge, a pale fill, an olive fill, a glow with a chip, a “Today ·” label), and the coach’s Week has none.The one mark a calendar must make the same everywhere.Ask 7
The free coach portal’s schedule wasn’t on the list; it is the one schedule that reads the device’s clock.Its delta is a defect, not a redesign.Ask 15, Ask 17
Stage 6c · the recipe · what is one recipe on every calendar, each line with its reason · Asks 1–12

The calendar recipe: thirteen lines, each with its reason

What every calendar in the app does the same way, written so a screen that lacks a line’s reason can see it and leave the line out (the rule this stage carries: a shared part travels with its reason). When ruled it becomes the calendar section of the product’s formatting standard, which Stage 8 owns. Where a line is already built somewhere, it names the screen it was taken from; nothing here is invented where the product already has an answer.

Recommended

The lines

“Today” names the screens that already do it; “Differs” the ones that would change, with who changes them.

Views mean one thing everywhere Ask 1

Week is seven days, Monday to Sunday, stepped with arrows. Month is a month grid that says what and when (on a team’s calendar) or how much (on the club’s). List is the surface’s natural range — a team’s season, the club’s week — and the date row says which. Day (a tournament) is one day. A phone drops a view that only repeats another.
Why: a person moves between these screens in one evening. If “Week” is seven days on the club calendar and a whole season on house league’s, the word stops meaning anything.
Today: coach, club, admin team, tournament. Differs: house league’s “Week” is a season in week groups (Stage 9).

A week starts on Monday, in every grid Ask 2

Week views, Month grids, week headings and a jump list all start on Monday.
Why: every week the product files already starts on Monday (the club calendar, the coach’s Week, house league, the public league); a Sunday-first Month puts a weekend tournament’s Saturday and Sunday on two rows, and disagrees with the Week one click away.
Today: the club calendar. Differs: the coach’s and the admin team’s Month grids (6c build); the public tournament’s jump list (tournament redesign).

Open on today, at every width Ask 3

A calendar opens on today when its range holds today; otherwise on the next day with something on it; a finished range on its last day. A season list opens with today at the top of its frame and the finished games above it.
Why: R3 (“today first, at every width”). The question every visit asks is “what’s next”; the phone already answers it, and the desk is the last exception (F01).
Today: the club, the tournament’s Day, the public tournament, the family app, the coach’s phone. Differs: the coach’s desk and the admin team (6c build); house league and the public league (Stage 9).

One toolbar line; the dates sit on it at a desk Ask 4

Under the title, one line. A scope that doesn’t depend on the view leads, as the olive pill (house league’s division: the 2026-10-07 order, scope first). Then the view switch. Then, wider than 900 px, the date arrows and the range: they follow the view because the view sets their unit (a week, a month, a day). Then filters, Search and Tools where the surface has them, then Export and the create button at the right end. A rare door (Import) lives in the create button’s menu or in Tools, never on the line. At 900 px and narrower the dates take their own row. On a phone the view switch is the glyph in the title row; Filter and Export share a row, and with no filter row Export is an icon in the title row.
Why: today the coach’s desk stacks three rows of controls above the first day. The tournament’s schedule built the one-line form on Oct 9 (the dates inline above 900, their own row below), so it is the shared part. “One Export and one create, above what they act on” is the portal’s ruling (2026-09-01) and an export sits above what it exports (2026-10-09).
Today: the club (except the dates, on their own row), the tournament (except Export and Add game, in its title band). Differs: the coach (6c build); the tournament’s title band (tournament redesign).

One booking row Ask 5

A list of bookings is the product’s row list (the portal’s row, the admin kit’s row: one recipe): one frame, a band per day or month, hairlined rows. The lead is the time (with the date when the list has no day bands); the title is who and what (“vs Lakeside”, “13U AAA · Practice”, the two teams); the caption is where, “Venue · Facility”, with the program’s word on a page that shows more than one program; the trail is the state and the score, then the chevron. A clash is 6a’s amber line under the place.
Why: the coach’s List and the tournament’s Day already wear it; it is the standard’s row list (§3.10). The club calendar’s table is the fourth shape for the same row, and its columns answer nothing a column answers (no total, no comparison down a column).
Today: the coach, the tournament’s Day and All games. Differs: the club calendar’s List and the admin team’s List (6c build); house league’s cards (Stage 9).

One chip in a calendar cell; a desk Month says what and when Ask 6

Inside a Week column or a Month cell a booking is one chip: the time on its first line, the title on its second, the kind’s colour on a one-team calendar, the team’s on the club’s, the amber flag for a clash. A desk Month cell shows up to three, then “+N more”, which opens the day. From 641 to 768 px and on a phone a Month is the touch Month: dots, the whole day taps, the chosen day’s rows underneath.
Why: the coach’s Month cuts a name to 14 letters with no time (F09); a Month that can’t say when isn’t worth opening. At 641–768 the tap floor is 44 px (K-12), and a chip in a 104 px cell can’t be 44 px tall, so the day itself must be the target.
Today: the club’s Week card is close (time, who, what · where). Differs: the coach’s and the admin team’s Month and Week chips (6c build). The club’s Month counts instead, on purpose (register R2).

One today mark; empty days stay as they are Ask 7

Today is the olive edge, and it is said in words wherever a day is headed, so it is never colour alone: a Week column’s border and top line under the heading “Today · Sat, Oct 10”, a Month cell’s ring, a phone day’s frame. In a list it is the day band “Today · Sat, Oct 10”, or, in a season list with nothing on today, a now line between the last finished row and the next (the timeline’s now line; never a band, which would head rows that aren’t today’s). Empty days keep what three calendars already share: “—” in a Week column, a bare Month cell, a run folded into one quiet line on a phone, nothing in a list.
Why: today is drawn five ways and the coach’s Week doesn’t mark it at all. The club’s olive edge and the tournament’s “Today ·” are the two that are built, ruled and measured.
Today: the club (Week, Month), the tournament (label). Differs: the coach (Week, Month, List), the admin team (6c build); the public tournament (tournament redesign).

One spelling for a day, a week and a range Ask 8

A day: “Sat, Oct 10” — over a Week column, on a band, as a phone day’s heading, as a day label. A heading or band wears the condensed display face in capitals (the 2026-09-28 ruling for column headings and bands), so the words stay one spelling and the style does the rest. In a sentence, “Saturday, October 10”. A row whose list has no day bands leads “Sat, Oct 10 · 2:00 p.m.”. A week: “Oct 5 – 11, 2026”, “Oct 26 – Nov 1, 2026”, “Dec 28, 2026 – Jan 3, 2027”; on a phone without the year. A month: “October 2026”. No “Week of …”. A place: “Venue · Facility”.
Why: one day is spelled seven ways today, three of them on the club calendar alone (“TUE 20”, “TUESDAY, OCTOBER 20”, “Tue, Oct 20”). “Sat, Oct 10” is the spelling most screens already use; the club’s range words are the shortest that can’t be misread.
Today: the family app, the tournament’s label and bands, most windows. Differs: almost everyone in one or two places (each delta names its owner).

One word for each state, and nothing hidden Ask 9

A scheduled booking says nothing. Otherwise one chip, one spelling: Moved, Postponed, Cancelled, Live, Final (where no team is “ours”), Win · Loss · Tie (a team’s own calendar, beside the score), Scrimmage, Forfeit. A cancelled booking is struck through and dimmed; a postponed one says Postponed. Neither is ever hidden from a schedule a person reads, and neither ever counts as a clash.
Why: “is it on?” is the question a schedule exists to answer. Hidden, a called-off game looks like an empty evening, and a postponed one like a game that’s on. Two spellings of one result for one team (Win and Won) is the spelling ruling’s bug.
Today: the coach (except “CANCELLED” written in capitals), house league (except Completed, and a Scheduled chip). Differs: the club calendar and the public league hide; the admin team says Won; the tournament says Playing now.

The clock is the booking’s own, said once Ask 10

Every date and time is read in the club’s zone (or a tournament game’s own stored clock), never the device’s; times read “2:00 p.m.” and ranges “5:30–7:30 p.m.”. The zone is said once, on the date row, in one sentence (“Times in Eastern time.”), read from the club’s zone rather than written into the page; it appears wherever a reader may sit outside it.
Why: R5 (a calendar entry is the event’s own time). Four screens still read the device’s clock, and three say three different things about which clock it is.
Today: the club calendar, the coach’s rows, house league. Differs: the free coach schedule, the coach’s tournament record, the public tournament’s calendar file, two Overview cards (Defects).

Export: one button, and Calendar wherever bookings are listed Ask 11

One Export (no chevron), Excel first, then CSV and Calendar (.ics) for any list of dated bookings, a PDF where a printed schedule exists; one line in the menu names what the file holds (“Oct 5 – 11, 2026 · 12 bookings, as shown”). A public or family schedule offers a subscription instead (6d).
Why: the 2026-10-01 and 2026-10-08 Export rulings, applied to calendars: the calendar file is the one format a schedule needs most, and the tournament’s schedule is the one admin calendar without it.
Today: the coach, the club, house league. Differs: the tournament (no Calendar); the coach’s phone (List only).

A booking opens a window that reads first Ask 12

A booking opens its window: it reads first (the record standard), says when, where and the state, and has one door to the booking’s own schedule. A reader who can’t change it gets no foot at all: no Done, no greyed-out form.
Why: the 2026-10-01 record standard and the 2026-10-09 rulings that took Done out of record windows.
Today: the club calendar, the tournament’s game window, the coach’s event window. Differs: the admin team’s window still has Done (6c build); house league opens a greyed “Edit Game” form for a reader (Stage 9).

On a phone: one frame per day, and every tool reachable Ask 12

A week stacks its days, each day one frame with its heading inside and its bookings as hairlined rows (the standard’s phone row list); a run of empty days folds into one quiet line; Month is the touch Month; every control is at least 44 px; Export is reachable from every view.
Why: the coach’s and the club’s phone weeks run on the same grouping and draw it two ways; the standard’s ruling P1 (2026-09-29) is one frame with hairlined rows, never a card per row. On the coach’s phone, Week and Month have no Export.
Today: the coach (except Export). Differs: the club’s phone week (6c build), the admin team (none at all).
Stage 6c · the register and the shared parts · what differs on purpose, and which part answers which question

What stays different on purpose, and the parts the calendars share

Two lists the formatting standard keeps beside the recipe. The first says where a calendar is allowed to differ and why, so nobody “fixes” it into sameness. The second lists every part two or more calendars wear, with the question it answers and the screens that ask that question. A screen that doesn’t ask the question doesn’t wear the part: that is how the club calendar’s phone came to copy two choices whose reasons it didn’t share.

Recommended

The deliberate-differences register

Each entry: what differs, where, and the reason that keeps it.
What differsWhereWhy it stays
R1 · List is a season on a team’s calendar, a week on the club’s, a day on a tournament’sCoach, admin team · club · tournamentEach is that reader’s unit of planning: a coach plans a season, a club shares its fields week by week, a director runs a day. The date row says which range is on screen.
R2 · The club’s Month counts bookings instead of naming themClub calendarA club’s day can hold twenty bookings; a count and an amber clash count answer “which days are busy, and which are broken”. A team’s day holds one or two, so its Month names them.
R3 · The tournament’s Timeline: the fields across a day, by the clockTournament schedulePlacing games on fields is its own job. Stage 11’s draft grid shares its shape (fields down, time across), not the Week’s.
R4 · Colour: the kind on a one-team calendar, the team on the club’sCoach, admin team · clubRuled 2026-10-09 (3): on one team’s calendar the question is what each event is; on the club’s it is whose. The kind is said in words on the club’s.
R5 · Family and public schedules read and never edit: no create, no Export, no clash marksFamily app, team page, public league, public tournament, ScoresA family asks “when and where”; a clash is the club’s question. A family takes the schedule with them by subscribing (6d), not by exporting a file.
R6 · The public tournament steps by game day, not by weekPublic tournamentAn event is a few dense days; empty days don’t exist there, so a strip of game days replaces arrows.
R7 · No Export on the admin team schedule, and its window has no editA team’s schedule (admin)The coaches keep that schedule (D3); the club calendar’s Team filter exports a range. A club admin doesn’t edit a team’s events.
R8 · Search, Filter and Tools on the tournament’s schedule onlyTournament scheduleAn event holds hundreds of games across divisions; a team’s season is about forty events, and the club calendar filters by venue, program and team.
R9 · A club-wide row shows the time as a range; a team’s shows the startClub calendar (and Stage 11) · coach, tournamentOn the club’s page the question is overlap, so the end matters; on a team’s or an event’s, the start is what a person arrives for.
R10 · The family reads sentences, not chips (“ · Cancelled”, “W 4–2”)Family app, team pageA family list is read, not scanned for states; the words are the recipe’s words in a sentence.
R11 · Date-grouped lists that are not calendars wear the words, not the viewsThe game-day board, the scorekeeper, the Overview’s tiles, the helper home, the club board’s next event, ScoresThey answer “what needs me now”, not “what’s when”; they take the recipe’s day words, clock and state chips (C8–C10) and nothing else.

The calendar-cell chipWhat’s in this day’s cell?Week columns and desk Month cells on a team’s calendar; the club’s WeekTwo chips today (the coach’s strip, the club’s card).

The zone sentenceWhich clock are these times in?Wherever a reader may sit outside the club’s zone: the club calendar now, every calendar once a club can be outside Eastern (S6-13)Written into one page; a different sentence on the public tournament.

The family’s schedule wordsWhat’s next for my child’s team?The family app, the public team page, the event window’s subtitleOne shared wording, already the recipe’s.

Not on the list on purpose: the tournament’s Timeline and Bracket (one surface each), the public tournament’s day strip (R6), house league’s Practices view (Stage 9 decides whether practices join its season list).

Stage 11’s draft grid: what it wears from the recipe, and why it isn’t the club calendar’s Week

The plan says the scheduler’s draft grid “is the club calendar’s Week view”. Drawn that way it would fail at its one job: a scheduler hands out time, and the Week stacks bookings as cards by day, with no hours and no empty slots. A free 8:00 slot on Lane 2 has no card to be. So the grid takes the Timeline’s shape (facilities down, the hours in each day) and wears the recipe’s lines around it. This specimen shows those lines only; the joint Stage 10 + 11 session designs the scheduler.

Stage 6c · the formatting check · every 6c drawing against the Coaches Portal’s written rules, before you see it

Formatting check

The benchmark is the written rules (the table and list standard, its exception register, the portal kit and the design log), not an earlier hub’s drawings. Each line says what the rule is, how the drawings meet it, and where the rules themselves need a sentence this stage writes.

Checked

The drawings against the rules

Rule (where it is written)The 6c drawings
A list is a row list: one painter of the ground, a band per group, hairlined rows, one lead mark, no rail (standard §3.10)Met: every List drawn (coach, club, admin team, house league, the public league) is one frame with day or month bands and hairlined rows. The club’s team swatch is its one lead mark (the 2026-10-09 colour rule), not a rail.
A calendar cell holds chips, not rows (register K-21)Met, and widened: K-21 named the coach’s chip only; the recipe makes the club’s Week card the same chip (time, then title). K-21’s line is rewritten when ruled.
A phone list keeps its frame; a card per row only for labelled lines (§3.10.8, ruling P1 2026-09-29)Met: the club’s phone week moves from a card per booking to the coach’s day frame. A booking has no labelled lines, so it isn’t a card.
641–768 is a touch band: the tap floor holds there (K-12)Met: the touch Month at 768 because a chip can’t reach 44 px in a month cell; the 768 frame’s buttons are 44 px icons.
One lime per screen (Stage 2, owner 2026-09-28)Met: Add Event, Add Game, Add game and Finalize are each their screen’s one lime; the club calendar has none.
One chip, uppercase mono (Ask 8 ruling 7)Met: Cancelled, Postponed, Live, Needs a score, Forfeit. The coach’s “CANCELLED”, written in capitals in its words, becomes “Cancelled” in the chip’s style: the same on screen, one spelling in the words.
Tinted panels retired; a callout is white with a coloured edge (2026-09-21)Met: today’s band in a list is an olive edge and olive words, not a tinted strip; the clash line is amber words.
Export is one button, Excel first; one line says what the file holds (2026-10-01, 2026-10-08)Met: unchanged menus; the tournament’s gains Calendar.
An export sits above what it exports; one Export and one create above the table (2026-10-09; the portal 2026-09-01)Met: Export and the create button at the toolbar line’s right end on every calendar.
A record reads first; a window that can’t be edited has no Done (2026-10-01, 2026-10-09)Met: the admin team schedule’s window loses Done; house league’s reader gets a read window.
The clock: “8:00 a.m.”, lowercase with periods (the spelling gate)Met: every drawn time.
Records with hyphens, scores with an en dash (Stage 2 formatting)Met: “3-2-1”, “2-1” on a record; “2–7” on a score.
Column headings and band rows take the condensed display face (Ask 8 ruling 1, 2026-09-28)Met after the design review: Week column headings and a phone day’s heading are in the display face, in capitals. The coach’s Week writes them in the body face today, so that is a delta too.
The olive face chooses what is read; a scope leads (2026-10-07)Met after the design review: house league’s division leads as the olive pill; Ask 13 settles the view’s three looks on that reason.
A status is said once (the standard’s summary rule)Met after the design review: the club List’s bands no longer repeat the clash count the pill and the rows already say.
A mark is never colour aloneMet after the design review: today is said in words wherever a day is headed.

Stage 6d · calendar feeds · item one of the gate: every door that puts a schedule into someone’s calendar, read from the code and counted on dev and production, 2026-10-11

Where the feeds stand: eight calendar doors, one that stays current, and nobody using it

A coach, a club admin and a family can each put a schedule into their own calendar today, but seven of the eight doors write a file: a snapshot that goes stale the first time a game moves. The one door that stays current is the family’s, and nobody can reach it: the family layer’s guardian switch is off until counsel signs off, and no team on either database has turned on Public link. This screen reads what exists before anything is drawn; the next five draw the doors, the window behind them, and what a subscribed event looks like in a calendar app.

As built · the feed itself

The one feed that exists, read line by line

One address, two kinds of link: a family’s own while they’re connected, and the team’s at Public link.
LineAs builtSo
Who may read itChecked on every read: the team’s visibility, a premium team, a club that hasn’t cancelled, the season live. No player names, no roster.Right, and kept for every feed.
The moment it writesThe event’s instant, anchored in universal time, so a calendar anywhere shows the right moment in its own zone.Right (the deep dive’s D-1 was the download, fixed 2026-09-25).
The linkStored only as a fingerprint, so it can be shown once. The family’s Subscribe makes a new link on every press and silently stops the one already in a calendar; the team-wide link can’t be shown on a public page without stopping every other subscriber’s. Ask 8: a link you can see again until you reset it.
How often it may be read240 reads an hour per caller address, across every feed. Calendar services read from shared servers. Ask 10: count per feed.
When it stops“Not found”. A calendar app keeps the last copy it read, so a removed coach, a reset link or a team closed to the public leaves the old events frozen in that calendar. Ask 9: a stopped link empties itself.
CachingFive minutes, private.Right: the calendar app is the slow part, not us.
The words“13U AAA — Practice”, always “vs”, “Arrive by 17:30”, a cancelled event dropped, no refresh hint, no name when empty. Specimen 5: the words every feed writes.

2 · What a coach’s feed carriesEverything on the coach’s schedule this season: every event, the organizer’s games not yet on the list, tryout days when they run them, with arrival, uniform and notes; cancelled kept and marked. (There are no staff-only events to add: S6D-06.)Specimen 1
3 · The family’s door while the guardian switch is offThe public team page, at Public link: a Subscribe button on its Schedule line, the page’s own address, no secret. Nothing at Families or Staff only. The family view’s own door drawn as it will be, waiting for counsel. Ruled: the first build leaves the family view untouched.Specimen 3
4 · The club calendar’s linkPersonal to the admin who makes it, revocable, carrying every booking the club calendar shows that person (not the page’s filters), four weeks back to six months ahead, no clash lines; never public. Ruled: deferred. Not in the first build: few readers, and the costliest feed to serve.Specimen 4
5 · How a cancelled event reads in a calendar appKept; marked cancelled the calendar file’s own way (Apple strikes it through) and “Cancelled · ” leading its title (Google draws no strike); shown as free time.Specimen 5

8 · A link you can see againThe Subscribe window shows the same link every time it opens, until Reset; it is signed, never stored readable. Its parts: three app doors, Copy, what’s in it, how often, last read, Reset at the body’s end. Revised: the last read is recorded at most once a day (“Read by your calendar today”).Specimen 2
9 · When a feed stops, or its season closesA link that stops answers with an empty calendar, so its events leave; a season’s feed carries the live season only, and the window says so.Specimens 2, 5
10 · Five fixes that ride with 6dCount reads per feed; the team page checks what the feed checks; help rewritten; a refresh hint and a name; an outside tournament as an all-day entry. Revised: a four-hour hint, not one hour; the public feed cached so it costs the same however many families subscribe; the per-feed limit writes nothing on a good read.Specimen 5, Not drawn
11 · Which plans carry the coach’s and the club’s feedsThe screens they live on: the coach’s Schedule (the Premium Coaches Portal and both Club bands; League Plus has no rep teams), the club calendar (League Plus and both Club bands). A packaging call: /strategy logs it.—

Subscribing is done about once a season, so it stays behind the door that’s already there rather than taking a place on the toolbar line.

What a coach’s feed carries, beside the download and a family’s feed

The coach’s feed is the coach’s screen; a family’s is the family list. Each feed carries what its reader already reads.
On the coach’s ScheduleThe download todayA coach’s feedA family’s feed (public or connected)
Games, practices, team eventsYesYesYes
A club’s schedule slot (Stage 11)Yes, as a practiceYes, as an ordinary practiceYes, as an ordinary practice
An outside tournament (its days, no time)A two-hour block at its start An all-day entry across its daysAn all-day entry across its days
The organizer’s games, not yet on the team’s listNo (S6D-05)YesNo: the family list doesn’t show them
Tryout daysNo (S6D-05)Only for a coach who runs tryouts (head coach)No
A cancelled eventMarked cancelledKept, marked (Ask 5)Kept, marked (today: dropped)
Arrival, in the clock’s spellingYesYesYes (today: “17:30”)
Uniform and the coach’s notesYesYesNo: the family list leaves them out
“Staff-only events” Don’t exist: an event has no visibility of its own, and a family reads every event the coach puts on the schedule. What a coach’s feed adds is the tryout days, the notes and uniform, and the organizer’s games.

The prompt’s shape listed “staff-only events, since it is the coach’s own”. Nothing in the schedule is hidden from families, so there is nothing of that kind to add. If the owner wants a staff-only event (a coaches’ meeting families shouldn’t see), that is a new kind of event and its own ask, not 6d’s.

One window answers everything a person needs to subscribe once and trust it: which app, what lands in it, how fresh it is, whether it’s working, and how to stop it. It reads first, like every record window: nothing in it is a form, and it has no foot. The coach’s is drawn here; the club admin’s and the family’s change only their words.

One part, four feeds: what changes between them

Everything not in this table is the same window.
LineA coachA club admin (deferred)A family (waits for counsel)The public team page
The doorSchedule › Export › Subscribe (desk); the calendar mark › Subscribe on this phoneCalendar › Export › SubscribeThe family view’s Schedule lineThe page’s Schedule line
The linkPersonal, one per team they coachPersonal, one per personPersonal, one per familyThe page’s own address: no secret, nothing to reset
What’s in itThe coach’s schedule (Ask 2)What the club calendar shows them (Ask 4)The family listThe family list
It stops whenThey leave the team or lose schedule access; ResetTheir calendar access ends; ResetTheir connection ends; ResetThe team leaves Public link, or the club cancels
Your calendar (last read)YesYesYesNo: it’s nobody’s
Reset the linkYesYesYesNo

“Shown again until reset” changes how a link is kept: today only a fingerprint is stored, so the window could show a link once. The recommended build signs the link instead (the server can rebuild it; a database read alone can’t), keeps a counter for Reset, and keeps the last read. That is new storage: one migration in the build, for the coach’s and the club admin’s links, which have nowhere to live today.

Stage 6d · specimen 3 · a family · the public team page (the one family door that can be live while the guardian switch is off) and the family view (waits for counsel) · Asks 3, 8, 10

A family subscribes from the team’s public page; the family view’s own door waits for counsel

A family reaches a team’s schedule without an account in one place: the team’s public page, when the coach has set the schedule to Public link. That page gains a Subscribe button above the schedule. Its feed is the page itself, so it needs no secret and nothing to reset. The connected family’s own door, in the family view, already exists and nobody can reach it: it is redrawn here as it will be, tagged as waiting for the guardian switch, and nothing drawn here turns that switch on.

A club admin keeps the club calendar in their own calendar app

Stage 6b shipped the club calendar’s download and handed its subscribable link here (6b, Ask 10). A club calendar link is a link to every booking the club runs, so it is personal: it carries what the club calendar shows the person who made it, across every program they can open, and it stops when their access does. The page’s filters shape a file, not a subscription: a subscription is the whole calendar that person can see. Clashes stay on the page, where they are worked.

Deferred 2026-10-11 Not in the first build (owner, after asking what feeds cost to serve): few people would hold one, and it is the costliest feed to serve. Drawn and ruled so a later build starts here.

Stage 6d · specimen 5 · in a calendar app · what a subscribed event looks like, and the words every feed writes · Asks 5, 9, 10

What a subscribed week looks like in someone’s own calendar

A feed’s whole job is the moment someone opens their own calendar and reads a block they didn’t type. These drawings are the calendar apps’, not ours, so each app draws the same feed its own way: Apple strikes a cancelled event through, Google draws no strike at all. That is why the cancelled word leads the title (Ask 5). The table under them is the recipe for a feed, from the 6c calendar recipe and Stage 11’s slots.

The words every feed writes

The 6c recipe (C8–C10) and Stage 11’s slots (plan §5.8), applied to a calendar entry. One home in the build, read by every feed.
The lineToday (the family feed)Why
F1 Title“13U AAA · Practice”, “13U AAA vs Oakridge Hawks”, “13U AAA @ Ridgeview Owls”, “13U AAA · Team photo day”. The club’s feed: the booking’s own words, as its file writes them (“Reds vs Blues”, “UAT Fall Invitational · 14 games”).“13U AAA — Practice”; always “vs”The team leads because a calendar holds many things; “@” is the recipe’s away (6c ruling).
F2 CancelledKept; “Cancelled · ” leads the title; marked cancelled; free time.DroppedAsk 5: Google draws no strike; a dropped event looks like an empty evening.
F3 PostponedNever written at its old time (the club feed’s league games).—As 6b’s file: a game at a time it won’t be played is worse than no entry.
F4 WhenThe event’s own moment; with no end entered, a game two hours, a practice an hour and a half; an outside tournament all day across its days.Right moment; tournament as two hoursS6D-08. One default per kind (the download writes two hours for everything).
F5 Where“Kinsmen Park · Diamond 2, 15 Main St”: the place, its facility, the street address.“Kinsmen Park, 2, 15 Main St”The recipe’s place (C8); the address lets the phone open directions.
F6 Notes“Arrive by 5:30 p.m. (Eastern time)”. A coach’s feed adds “Uniform: …” and the event’s notes. A club slot adds nothing.“Arrive by 17:30”The clock’s spelling; the zone because the reader may be elsewhere (C10).
F7 A link backA coach’s: the event in the portal. The club’s: the booking on the club calendar. The public feed’s: the team page.NoneOne tap from the calendar to the whole story.
F8 The calendarNamed “13U AAA · UAT Rep Club” (the club’s: “UAT Rep Club calendar”) even when empty; a refresh hint of four hours (owner 2026-10-11: a dial, lowered only with the stack-health numbers in hand).No name when empty; no hintS6D-11: Outlook and Apple read a hint; Google ignores it, so help says “up to a day”.
F9 What it spansA team’s feed: the live season only. The club’s: four weeks back to six months ahead.The live seasonAsk 9 and Ask 4.
F10 When it stopsA link that stops (reset, removed, closed to the public, the club cancelled, the season closed with none after it) answers with an empty calendar under its name, so its events leave. A link never made answers “not found”, as now.“Not found” for every caseS6D-04: an app keeps the last copy of a feed that won’t answer, frozen.

Each event keeps the same identity in every read, so a calendar moves an existing block rather than adding a second one (as built). A season’s close empties its feed (S6D-12): the season’s past games leave the subscribed calendar and the next season’s arrive when it starts. That follows the one-page ruling for a closed season; the window tells a subscriber in one line (“This season only”).

One build, three commits

Ask 12, with Asks 4, 8 and 10 as ruled. The build prompt: CLUB_TIER_STAGE6D_BUILD_PROMPT.md.
PartWhat
Part 0 · the recordThe rulings into the design log; the feed recipe F1–F10 as the standard’s §11.4; the three sentences (a)–(c).
Part A · the feedA coach’s feed (new) and the public team page’s feed (new, at the page’s own address), and the family’s existing feed, all on the recipe’s words and re-checked on every read; a coach’s link signed and shown again until reset, its last read recorded once a day; one migration for the coach’s links (the never-used team-wide link column retires in it); a stopped link empties itself; a per-feed read limit that writes nothing on a good read; the public feed cached so every family shares one read; the team page and the feed asking one question; the outside tournament all day; a four-hour hint and the name.
Part B · the doorsThe shared Subscribe window and phone sheet; the coach’s Export row and the phone’s Calendar drawer; the public page’s button and its choices; help rewritten (the “planned for a future release” answer; a coach’s “Subscribe to your team’s schedule”; a line for families on the public page’s feed).
Not in this buildThe club admin’s feed (Ask 4, deferred); the family view’s door (waits for counsel). Both stay drawn here.
WalksA real subscription in Google, Apple and Outlook (a moved event moves, a cancelled one reads as off, Reset empties the old one); a removed coach’s calendar empties; a team set back to Families empties its public subscribers.
Ruled 2026-10-11

What feeds cost to serve, and what keeps it cheap

The owner’s question before ruling. An estimate from the code, not a measurement: the morning stack-health check measures it once feeds are live.

One calendar check costs about what one family opening the team’s schedule page costs: nine small lookups and, today, one write. The file is 10–30 KB. Calendar apps check on their own timer, spread through the day: no Saturday-morning peak. Load grows with subscriptions × how often apps check, not with how busy anyone is.

SubscriptionsTypical (about 8 checks a day each)Worst case (every app hourly)
100About 800 a day, one every 2 minutesAbout 2,400 a day
1,000About 8,000 a day, one every 11 secondsAbout 24,000 a day
5,000About 40,000 a day, one every 2 secondsAbout 120,000 a day, about one a second
ControlWhat it saves
The public team feed is cached (one address per team, identical for every family)Fifteen families on one team cost about one check every few minutes, however many subscribe. A private link per family could not be shared this way: a further reason for Ask 3.
A four-hour refresh hint, not one hourApple and Outlook would otherwise check about hourly. A moved game takes a little longer to reach them; Google already takes up to a day.
The last read recorded once a dayNo write per check for “Read by your calendar today”.
A per-feed read limit that writes nothing on a good readToday’s counter writes a row on every check and counts by address, which would also cut off every feed read through one of Google’s shared servers (S6D-03).
The club admin’s feed deferredThe costliest read (the club calendar’s, built for one page view), for the fewest people (S6D-13).

A feed is never how an urgent change reaches anyone: a game moved two hours before it starts may not reach Google in time. The app and its notices stay the source; the window’s “How often” line says so plainly.

Stages 10 + 11 · where the club’s time stands · read from the code and both databases, 2026-10-10

Nothing holds the club’s time today, and the precedents are narrower than the plan assumed

Before drawing, every part these stages touch was read in the code: the venue book, the clash rule, the calendar, how a tournament game reaches a team, house league’s practices, the feeds, the tournament generator as built, sending, money. Twelve findings came out of it. Three of them change what was drawn: the Timeline’s shape, what the tournament generator can actually share, and when a club slot reaches a team.

On this screen:
Read from the code

What exists today, part by part

Five read-only surveys of dev at 43678430, 2026-10-10. Each row: what the code does, and what it means here.
PartWhat the code does todayWhat it means for Stages 10 + 11
The venue bookVenues and their facilities (name, kind, order, notes); Archive; server-only writes. No contact, no sport on a facility.A permit and a schedule pick from it. The venue gains one field, a bookings contact (Ask 7).
Time the club holdsNothing. No table for a permit, block, slot, booking or club schedule. The club’s time is only the bookings themselves, in five tables.Both stages are new. One model of time (ruled): a permit’s blocks and a schedule’s blocks are the same record.
The clash rule (6a)Two answers, booked by and busy then; never refuses. A “permit hook” comment says a third kind needs no caller changed, but the callers filter the two kinds by name, and a booking against a permit is not a pair.The permit line is built beside the pair rule, as its own quiet line (Ask 3). Two teams sharing one lane in one slot would read as a clash: the build must say they don’t.
The club calendar (6b, 6c)Reads rep events, tryout days, league games and practices and the club’s tournament games directly; read-only; one window of up to 42 days.A slot written as a real practice row needs nothing new here; the read window gains a door to its schedule.
A rep team’s scheduleThe tournament mirror writes a published game onto each team, read-only to the coach, the server refuses a change to its time or place; the coach keeps arrival, notes, attendance, lineup. It writes when someone opens the schedule, not when the game is published. No hand-back exists. Every event belongs to one season.A club slot follows the mirror’s rules but is written when the schedule is sent (P11-05), lands in the team’s running season (Ask 15), and gains a hand-back (Ask 17).
House league’s practicesMade by hand; only cancelled afterwards; no source or creator; written by the owner and a league admin only (a club admin is refused); families never see a practice (no public view, no feed, no notice).A schedule-made practice needs a source link and a writer the schedule runs; recommended with Stage 9 (Ask 6).
The team’s feedThe family feed drops cancelled events and needs a guardian link the switch keeps off; the team-wide feed is unused; a coach downloads a file. Today a club slot could reach a family only through the team’s public page.6d settles the feed before the scheduler is built.
The tournament generator (built Oct 9)Two steps (settings → ranked drafts with one statement of what saving does), the kit’s wide window. Its own header: “nothing here is shared yet”. The engine pairs two-sided games of one length, and treats evening slots as poor ones.The scheduler wears the frame and the look; its engine is its own (Ask 5).
The tournament TimelineFacilities across, time down, one day; a column only where a game stands; an empty slot is never drawn. Drag with a preview, a red refusal with its reason, Undo for 8 seconds.The ruling’s words say “fields down, time across”. The grid takes specimen 4’s layout and the Timeline’s behaviour (Ask 12).
SendingNothing sends to the club’s staff. Stage 3a’s reminders are the full pattern: a preview per team, who can’t be reached and why, a sample, “Last sent … by …”, a lock against a double send, reply-to the sender. No email carries an attachment; every PDF is drawn in the browser.The send copies the reminders (Ask 7, Ask 9). The bookings contact reads the schedule in the email’s body for now.
MoneyBudget words already include Facilities › Diamond Permits, Dome Time, Cage or tunnel rental, Indoor space. An entry carries a word, not a line. Allocate draws from a line. By sessions already splits by each team’s count.A permit names its budget line (Ask 8a). A split by the time each team got is Bill the teams, in the first cut (Ask 23, which brought Ask 8b forward).

What the numbers say: no customer holds a venue, a permit or a house league on production, so nothing migrates and nothing breaks. Facility time is real money on production today, and it sits in the teams’ budgets, on no schedule: coaches rent their own dome time and nobody books it as an event. These stages assume the club holds the time and hands it out, which is right for a club. A team that rents its own time keeps doing what it does today.

Stages 10 + 11 · the one model · ruled 2026-10-08

One model of the club’s time: a permit holds it, a schedule hands it out, every program reads the result

Before the screens, the idea they share. A permit and a schedule are not two features: they are the time the club holds, and how that time is handed out. Each screen after this is one step of this line.

Ruled 2026-10-08 · Stage 11 Ask 2

A block of time: what a permit records and a schedule hands out

Never two models of the club’s time.

A permit

The time the club holds: blocks (a venue, a facility, the days, the hours, the dates), dates off, the issuer, the reference, the cost, the document. “Fall diamonds 2026”: Lions Park · Diamond 2 · Tue, Thu · 5:30–9:00 p.m. · Sep 8 – Oct 29.
→

A schedule

The same blocks, picked from the permit in one choice (or entered where the club holds none), cut into slots: a slot length, a changeover, how many teams share one facility at once. Each slot is given to a team. Kept by name.
→

Sent

Each slot becomes a practice on its team’s schedule, read-only to the coach (ruled). House league’s practices join with Stage 9 (Ask 6).
→

Read by

The club calendar · the clash check · the permit’s use (“51.5 of 80 h”) · the team’s feed (6d) · the bill by the time each team got (Ask 23). Nothing keeps a copy of its own.

What this saves a club: the dome’s contract is entered once. The schedule starts from it, the coaches see the result, and at renewal the permit shows how much of it was used, all read from one set of bookings. Without the shared block, the club would type the dome’s hours twice, and the two copies would drift at the first change.

Stages 10 + 11 · specimen 1 · Organization › Venue library · Asks 1, 2, 4, 7

The Venue library becomes the club’s venues and the time it holds at them

Where should a permit live? The prompt recommended “on the venue it covers”. The code and the way towns issue permits push that one step further. A permit is the club’s own record, because one permit can cover several parks. It lists on a Permits view beside the venues, and each venue’s window shows the permits that hold time there.

Stages 10 + 11 · specimen 3 · the clash check’s second question · Ask 3

The clash check learns one more thing: is this time inside a permit the club holds?

Stage 6’s check answers “does this collide with another booking?”. Permits add a second question, and it is quieter: nobody else is on the diamond, but the club may not hold that time. It warns where the booking can still change, and it never blocks.

Stages 10 + 11 · specimen 6 · a schedule’s page · Asks 12, 13

A week of the winter dome, every slot on the page, and whether it is fair beside it

This is the screen the owner described: adjust by hand after it generates, like a tournament director can. It shows a week, because a winter of dome nights repeats by the week. It shows every slot, because handing out time means seeing the time nobody has yet.

On this screen:
The precedent · as built

The precedent: the tournament’s Timeline, as built 2026-10-09

A capture at true size (1440): one day, the fields across, the hours down.

Read against the ruling: “the Timeline’s shape” was written as “fields down, time across”. The Timeline is the other way round, and shows one day. A column exists only where a game stands, and free time is blank space, never a slot. A scheduler drawn on it could not show a week of dome nights or an open slot (finding P11-01). What it shares with the grid below is the question (place time by facility and clock) and the behaviour (drag with a preview, a refusal that says why, Undo).

To Dana Whitfield, Sam Ortiz · Subject Winter dome 2026–27: 15U AAA’s slots
Hi Dana and Sam,

The club has given 15U AAA 36 slots at Lakeshore Dome, from Mon, Jan 4 to Sun, Mar 28, 2027:
  • Mondays, 7:00–8:00 p.m. · Lane 1
  • Tuesdays, 6:00–7:00 p.m. · Lane 2
  • Wednesdays, 8:00–9:00 p.m. · Lane 1
No slot on Mon, Feb 15 (Family Day): that week your Monday moves to Thu, Feb 18, 8:00 p.m. · Lane 2.

They’re on 15U AAA’s schedule now. Your families see them there.
